headline: Folding and the StyleX compiler both delete the styling component on flat JSX, so the spread that remains is serialization: `next-yak-9.7` renders 0.578 ms/1k against `emotion`'s 2.85, and among the zero-runtime lanes the fastest is whoever writes the fewest class bytes.

top3.label: StyleX without CSS layers (:not() specificity hack)

microbench.why: Static folding rewrites `<DenseButton>` to a plain `<button className>`, so no styling component renders and `next-yak-9.7`'s library slice falls to 0.311 ms; `stylex-layers` reaches the same floor from the compiler side. Of what is left, `emotion` is the outlier at 2.85 ms/1k: 5.22 ms of its 7.76 ms render sits in its own packages and `murmur2` alone is 101 ms of a 224 ms JS window, hashing the serialized rule once per instance. The zero-runtime lanes then separate on markup rather than styling. `stylex-layers` writes 548 B of HTML per instance with 8-character hashed classes, `bamboo` writes 1.10 kB because its class names spell out the declaration and carry 11 HTML-escaped characters per instance into the attribute, and that alone puts it at 1.07 ms/1k against StyleX's 0.440.

autocannon.why: Serving the same button over HTTP reproduces the SSR ordering. `next-yak-9.7` and `next-yak-css-9.7` answer 596 and 593 req/s against `vanilla`'s 524, because the folded markup (165 B per instance) is shorter than the hand-written class names it replaces. Class bytes then set the rest of the field: `stylex-layers` holds 413 req/s while `bamboo` manages 198 and `panda` 164 on the same atomic model with readable names. `emotion` at 128 req/s re-hashes on every request.

attribution.why: react-dom does nearly all the work in the fast lanes, so the split is a bytes-written contest: `next-yak-css-9.7` spends 27.9 ms of its 38.1 ms JS window in react-dom, leaving a 0.345 ms library slice. `emotion` inverts that with 5.22 ms of library self-time against 1.87 ms of React, and `styled-components` puts 4.23 ms into `generateAndInjectStyles` and stylis. `bamboo` has no styling slice at all, its own package costing 8.80 ms where `vanilla`'s component module costs 7.62, yet its react-dom slice climbs to 85.5 ms writing and escaping the atomic class attribute, which is how a zero-runtime lane still lands at 3.41 ms.

hydrate.why: Every extracted lane ships its sheet as a static file, so hydration is pure JS and the span records 0 ms of style, layout and paint. `styled-components` and `goober` inject during hydration instead and the browser answers inside the span (0.457 ms of recalc plus a 0.609 ms layout for `styled-components`), which puts both at 169 ms against the 61-64 ms cluster; `emotion` at 124 ms serializes on the client as well. The top of the fast cluster spans 1%, well under the run-to-run spread.

inp.why: Re-rendering one button separates the lanes that recompute a class from the ones that swap a string. The build-time field lands at 6.8-8.3 ms, with `vanilla` and `next-yak-css-9.7` at the bottom and `bamboo` and `stylex-layers` at 7.6. `emotion` needs 31.5 ms, `goober` 22.7 and `styled-components` 16.8, each re-deriving the class for a single element. The 9.6.0 runtime's 13.3 ms is its `Yak` wrapper repeating its bookkeeping.

mount.why: Cold mount parses the sheet and paints once, so the runtime lanes pay their first injection here: `styled-components` mounts in 172 ms and `goober` in 171 against the 116-118 ms floor that the folded, StyleX, `bamboo` and `vanilla` builds share. `emotion` at 191 ms is the slowest of the shipped defaults, building its cache before first paint. The floor lanes differ by under 1.5%, which is noise.

renderTiming.why: Chrome recalculates style once for every lane and lays out once, so the counts cannot separate them and the ordering falls to the recalc's own cost, 0.362-0.517 ms. One static sheet costs the same whoever authored it, and no lane forces a synchronous layout.

payload.why: The css-prop fold concatenates the whole rule set into one class and ships 3.95 kB gzipped, under `vanilla`'s 4.44 kB of hand-written names. Atomic naming is what costs bytes, since every rule is written twice, once in the sheet and once in the markup: `stylex-layers` ships 9.10 kB with hashed classes and `bamboo` 12.0 kB with readable ones. The utility lanes are worst, `tailwind-merge` at 21.4 kB and `cnfast` at 22.4 kB.

nsweep.why: Scaling the button to 4000 instances keeps the zero-runtime lanes linear and separates them only by per-instance markup: `stylex-layers` 4.77 ms, `vanilla` 4.81 and `next-yak-css-9.7` 4.85 are one measurement. The per-render libraries multiply their own work by n, `emotion` reaching 29.3 ms and `styled-components` 20.6, while `bamboo`'s 11.3 ms is class bytes times n rather than styling work.

crossCase: `realistic-button` is the depth-1 anchor of the composition ladder (the Examples `compose-1`, `compose-3` and `compose-6` below). Folding, not the perf runtime, is the whole win here: it deletes the styling component, and switching it off costs 65% (0.953 against 0.578 ms/1k). Under composition the split reverses, the perf runtime carries the load and folding leaves a residual wrapper at the `styled(Component)` seam.
